Serena and Djokovic I believe are the only two players to win four Majors in a row since Graf did it in 88. In singles at least. Their accomplishments were respectively called the SERENASLAM and the Nole Slam. Djokovic was a match away from a CYGS as we call it on the tennis reddit in 2023 when he lost the 2023 USO Final.

What makes all this interesting is that the idea of "Winning the Grand Slam" now specifically means winning all four in one calendar year, but what wasn't the original meaning of the term. The journalist who first coined the term specifically envisioned it as meaning winning four in a row, so by the original definition both Serena and Djokovic accomplished that.

The term itself comes from bridge. Perhaps someone who knows bridge better than I do can correct me, but I believe a grand slam in bridge means completing all 13 tricks in a hand. The terms in tennis and baseball similarly mean clearing the board, whether by winning all four majors or by driving four runners home.

A short walk down the halls of the history of mathematics.

Fermat's famous "Last Theorem" states that the equation (a^n + b^n = c^n) has no whole number solutions for a, b, and c when the power n is greater than 2.  (When n=2, there are infinite solutions, each called a Pythagorean triplet, such as [3,4,5] or [5,12,13].)

He wrote in his copy of Diophantus's "Arithmetica", "I have discovered a truly marvelous proof of this proposition that this MARGIN is too narrow to contain."
[N.B. the singular "MARGIN".]

No one has ever found his "marvelous proof".  The theorem was proven by Andrew Wiles in 1994, but no one would call this proof "a truly marvelous proof", except for the fact that it was a proof that had been sought for centuries.

"In couplets, one line often makes a  point
Which hinges on its bending, like a joint;
The sentence makes that line break into two.
Here's a CAESURA: see what it can do.
(And here's a gentler one, whose pause, more slight,
Waves its two hands, and makes what's left sound right.)"--

--The great American poet John Hollander wrote a handbook on verse entitled *Rhyme's Reason*, in which he explains verse forms through self-referential examples. (Hollander makes a distinction between "verse," which is form, and "poetry," which concerns content, rhetorical devices included.)

***
In Classical poetry, the most distinctive use of the caesura is in elegiac couplets, which are usually described as a six-ffot line followed by a five foot line, but might be better thought of as a six-foot line followed by two two-and-a-half-foot lines. 

Here's an example in English, written by Samuel Taylor Coleridge, when he wasn't hanging around in Xanadu:

"In the hexameter rises the fountain's silvery column;
In the pentameter, aye   falling back in melody." 

Both JH and STC do a good point in describing the effect the device has on the reader, I think.

(Part 1) 

I don’t know what “easification” means in this context. That’s not a term we use. 

But I can take a stab at this. 

If you’re referring to the difficulty of say, the Midi, all the puzzles are supposed to be about the same level of difficulty. Of course, there’s always going to be something that plays harder, but every puzzle should feel like an early-week Daily crossword difficulty. 

The Daily gets progressively harder, starting on Monday, peaking in difficulty on Saturday. The Sunday puzzle is larger, but about the same difficulty as a Thursday. We’re not intentionally making puzzles easier. If you solve, say, a Saturday daily puzzle from 2026, it’s probably going to be easier than a Saturday daily puzzle from 1996. It’s not because the puzzle got easier, it’s just that the references in the clues and answers are more topical and top-of-mind for a solver than something from 30 years ago. 

continued ...

@The X-Phile

Part 2 

If this question is about how to make a crossword “easier” or “harder,” the difficulty can come from four different areas: 
(1) The clues, which I can slide in difficulty. If the answer is ROCK with the clue [Classic rock cover?], that’s a Saturday-level clue. If it’s [Scissors topper, in a game], that’s a Monday-level clue.
(2) The answers. Proper nouns are harder in general as they are know-it-or-you-don’t. Easier puzzles should have more accessible vocabulary.
(3) The grid shape. In general, the more “open” a crossword is, the harder it is for solvers. Larger swaths of letters are harder to solve. Insider crossword alert! When there’s a diagonal black square “staircase” running from the upper-right to lower-left, the puzzle will be easier than a staircase running from the upper-right to lower-left. The reason is because in the former example, a scrabbly letter like “J” can start both words. In the latter example, it’s harder to have a word end with a “J” and start with a “J” on the same square. 
(4) In general, a larger puzzle is “harder” because it takes longer to solve than a small puzzle. A 5x5 Mini will almost always be easier than a 15x15 daily.

The Times wanted to make an original logic puzzle for a long time. Logic puzzles — unlike the English-centric focus of many of our games — appeal to a wide audience and reach beyond non-native English speakers. So, there was a big, untapped audience for a game like Pips. 

Pips was born out of an internal “game jam” — essentially a hackathon for games. The early version was low-tech — paper and pen and physical dominos! Games are pitched, and a select few like Pips, make it through the multiple rounds of testing. It was originally pitched in 2024, went live in beta in Canada in early 2025, and was released globally in August, 2025.

We’re always looking at new games, so stay tuned!

@Vaer 

(Part 1)

Good questions!

I make 2-3 Midi puzzles per week, and fill in the other 4-5 from contributors. 

A little background: The Daily crossword has an open submission policy — anyone can submit a puzzle. But that means we receive about 200 submissions/week, and it takes all seven editors to cull through the submission pile. Since I’m the only editor who works on the Midi, it’s simply not feasible for me to comb through 800+ submissions/month by myself from outside contributors. At the same time, it’s also unreasonable to expect I should make all Midis myself. Cluing and filling a grid (at least for me!) doesn’t take *that* long, but theme generation does. I spend a lot of time exploring possible themes, many of which don’t make it to the solver. It’s challenging to create themes that are fun, novel, and most importantly, accessible to new solvers. So, we settled on a happy medium of working with known contributors. 

We started with a small crew of 15 puzzlemakers spread over 13 bylines. These were constructors I knew from their daily puzzles, and all the constructors have fun ideas, write good clues and can fill a grid up to Midi standards. Every contributor has a certain specialty – expert clue writer, super creative ideas, amazing smooth grid filler, etc. Ideally, each constructor is good at everything, but it’s nice to have a variety. We’re starting to mix in new voices, too, which keeps things fresh for solvers.
